one_liner: Header-only RecSplit MPHF: 1.8 bits/key, smaller than CMPH's CHD and about 2x faster to build and query on 1e9 keys.
what_it_does: Builds a static minimal perfect hash function: a bijection from a fixed set of n distinct keys onto 0..n-1, so per-key data can sit in a plain array. sux::function::RecSplit<LEAF_SIZE, AllocType> is a class template you construct from a std::span<const std::string>, a newline-delimited ifstream, or a span of pre-hashed 128-bit keys, plus a bucket size. mph(key) returns the index. The interface has nothing in common with CMPH's C API (no cmph_config/cmph_search, no runtime algorithm choice), and saving/loading goes through operator<< and operator>> on iostreams.
how_it_is_fast: Keys are hashed once to 128 bits with SpookyHash and bucketed, b keys per bucket on average (5 to 2000). Each bucket is split recursively: fanout 2 at the top, then fixed-size groups, down to leaves of at most LEAF_SIZE keys. At every node a brute-force search finds a seed that splits the keys exactly (at leaves, one that maps them bijectively). Only the seeds are stored, as Golomb-Rice codes whose parameters are tables computed at compile time, and a double Elias-Fano list gives each bucket's key offset and bit position. A lookup is therefore one Elias-Fano access plus a short walk down one bucket's tree, using multiply-shift range reduction and broadword select (BMI2 pdep/tzcnt when compiled for it). The RecSplit paper (ALENEX 2020) reports 1.56 bits/key this way, 8.3% above the 1.44 bits/key lower bound.
when_to_use: Static key sets of millions to billions of keys (URLs, k-mers, dictionary terms) that are built once and queried many times, where the MPHF must be small: about 1.8 bits/key at LEAF_SIZE=8, b=100, down to 1.56 bits/key at LEAF_SIZE=16, b=2000.

Replacing CMPH's CHD in C++ code: on 1e9 random 64-bit keys RecSplit l=8,b=100 is smaller (1.80 vs 2.01-2.17 bits/key), builds 2.1-25x faster and answers lookups in about half the time (204 vs ~417 ns).

When you want to tune space against build time: LEAF_SIZE (a template parameter) and bucket size cover the range from 233 s at 2.95 bits/key (l=5, b=5) to 936 s at 1.80 bits/key (l=8, b=100) on 1e9 keys.
Read-heavy services that query one built instance from many threads: operator() is const and has been thread-safe since 1.0.1.
Linux servers with large key sets, where AllocType::TRANSHUGEPAGE or FORCEHUGEPAGE puts the structure on huge pages; switching takes one template argument.
when_not_to_use: Latency-bound lookups: about 200 ns/key at 1e9 keys in the PTHash paper's Table 5, against 37-64 ns for PTHash at 3-4 bits/key.

When the build must be fast or parallel at very low space: this construction is single-threaded, and the GpuRecSplit README measures it at about 1.2 ms/key for l=16, b=2000 (1.56 bits/key), against 138 us/key for single-threaded SimdRecSplit.

Dynamic sets or membership tests: the structure is immutable (any change means a full rebuild), and keys outside the set map to arbitrary valid indices (issue #21), so you must store your own fingerprints to reject them.

Key sets that don't fit in RAM: this implementation holds all 128-bit hashes in memory (16 bytes/key, about 16 GB for 1e9 keys) and sorts them. The paper's external-memory construction is not implemented here.
Windows/MSVC builds: the headers need POSIX sys/mman.h, GCC/Clang builtins and attributes, and variable-length arrays, and CI builds only on Ubuntu x86-64.

integration.dependencies: none (SpookyV2.hpp is bundled; googletest only for the test suite)
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (std::span, since PR #23 in Oct 2024); GCC or Clang; __int128 support for more than 2^32 keys
integration.platforms: POSIX. x86-64 has BMI/BMI2 fast paths with portable fallbacks, and an aarch64 build fix was merged in 2022 (PR #15). CI covers only Ubuntu 24.04. The PTHash mphf_benchmark harness disables RecSplit on __APPLE__.
integration.thread_safety: Concurrent lookups on a built instance are safe (NEWS 1.0.1; const operator() since PR #22). Construction runs on a single thread.

gotchas: Duplicate keys make the constructor loop forever (documented in the header, and issue #20 was closed as won't-fix), so deduplicate first.

The hash128_t constructor assumes uniformly random 128-bit hashes and sorts your span in place. Structured values such as hash128_t(0, i) overflow the fixed 3000-key bucket limit and segfault (issue #7). Hash integer keys first, e.g. with first_hash(&key, sizeof key) as mphf_benchmark does.

Compile with -DNDEBUG: the code is 'heavily asserted', and without it the Elias-Fano constructor re-checks every bucket. Errors come as assert/abort, never exceptions: loading a file saved with another LEAF_SIZE calls abort(). The serialized format is raw host-endian binary with no version field.

Header hygiene: 'using namespace std' inside sux::function, global macros (likely, unlikely, first_hash, skip_bits, ALLOW_UNALIGNED_READS) and a global SpookyHash class can collide with other code in a large codebase.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when you want the authors' small, dependency-free reference RecSplit that you can copy into an include path at about 1.8 bits/key. Take SimdRecSplit/GpuRecSplit for the same structure with 8-50x faster (and multi-threaded) construction, ShockHash or ConsensusRecSplit below about 1.6 bits/key, PTHash for 3-5.5x faster lookups at 3-4 bits/key, and emphf when 2.61 bits/key with a 374 s build at 1e9 keys fits better than RecSplit's 1.80 bits/936 s or 2.95 bits/233 s.
verified_claims_summary: In the PTHash authors' mphf_benchmark (Table 5 of the SIGIR'21 paper): 1e9 uniformly random 64-bit keys, one core of an i9-9900K, gcc 9.2.1 -O3 -march=native. RecSplit l=8,b=100 built in 936 s at 1.80 bits/key with 204 ns lookups; CMPH's CHD took 1972-23746 s (lambda 4-6) for 2.01-2.17 bits/key with ~417 ns lookups. At 1e8 keys the same table shows a smaller build gap (92 s vs 121 s for CHD lambda=4; lookups 124 vs 204 ns). The harness pins a May 2020 sux commit (before the BMI2-detection fix that PR #16 says speeds queries by 10-20%) and builds CMPH through its own autotools configure.
status_note: Stale: the master branch is unchanged since October 2024 and the last release is 1.0.4 (June 2023). A May 2026 'bench' branch commit touches only Elias-Fano/select, not RecSplit. There are no open issues, and this is the algorithm authors' own header-only code under GPLv3 plus the GCC Runtime Library Exception ('use it everywhere, exactly like libstdc++'), though RecSplit.hpp still carries a leftover LGPLv3 paragraph, which is why GitHub reports NOASSERTION.
